rounds.s: A short call about your background, the role and the next steps.
look: Introduction
Who you are, what you do now and what you are best at, in about a minute.
Resume
Two or three projects, the stack and the impact, with numbers.
Role and team fit
Why this role, what you want next, what kind of team suits you.
Logistics
Timeline, location, notice period, other processes, compensation range.
prep: Write a 60 to 90 second pitch and say it out loud until it sounds natural.
Pick the two projects you will talk about in every round, with one number each.
Know your notice period, your timeline and the range you are aiming for before the call.
Have two questions ready about the team and the process.

rounds.s: Solve one or two problems in a shared editor, talking as you go.
look: Data structures and algorithms
Arrays, strings, hash maps, trees, graphs, heaps, dynamic programming.
Problem solving
Correct, efficient, clean code; you test it yourself.
Complexity
Time and space, said without being asked.
Follow-ups
Edge cases, a faster or smaller version, what changes if the input does not fit in memory.
prep: Use the same seven steps every time (below) so you never freeze.
Say the complexity of every solution before the interviewer asks.
Test with an empty input, one element and a large or tricky case.
Do one problem a day from the coding track.

rounds.s: Design a system end to end, then defend trade-offs and handle failures and scale.
look: Scalable systems
An end-to-end design for a real problem, from requirements to data flow.
APIs, storage and caching
The API, the data model, SQL or NoSQL, what to cache and how data moves.
Trade-offs and bottlenecks
What you chose, what you rejected and why; where it breaks first.
Reliability and scale
What happens when a box, a zone or a dependency fails, and at ten times the load.
prep: Start with requirements and a quick estimate (QPS, storage, bandwidth).
Draw the high-level design first: clients, gateway, services, storage, cache, object storage.
Go deep on one or two parts the interviewer cares about.
End with failures, scale and what you would do next.

rounds.s: Read an existing piece of code, find and fix bugs, improve it and explain your changes. An AI assistant may be allowed.
look: Understand the code
Read it and say what it does before changing anything.
Find and debug
Spot the bug, name the input that shows it, fix it, handle the edge cases.
Improve
Make it clearer or faster without changing what it does.
Explain
Say why each change is right and what you would test. With AI, how you used it matters more than the answer.
prep: Read top to bottom once, then say in one sentence what the function promises.
Find the input that breaks it before you fix it: that becomes your first test.
Change as little as needed to fix it; improve it separately.
If AI is allowed, give it the code, the failing input and what you expect, then check what it says.

rounds.s: Stories from your work that show impact, collaboration, how you handle difficulty and leadership.
look: Impact and ownership
You saw a problem, took it on and drove it to a result.
Collaboration
How you work with other teams and with people you disagree with.
Handling challenges
Ambiguity, failure, pressure: what you did and what you learned.
Leadership mindset
Influence without a title, mentoring, starting things.
Values
Care for users, doing the right thing long term, including others. Google calls this Googleyness.
prep: Write 6 to 8 stories in STAR form: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Tag each story with what it shows; one story can answer several questions.
Say I, not we, for your part; end with a number and what you learned.
Keep each story to about two minutes out loud.

rounds.s: How you work with others and decide, plus a technical deep dive into a project you led.
look: Collaboration
Working with different teams and stakeholders.
Ownership
Taking initiative and finishing what you start.
Communication
Explaining complex ideas clearly to different audiences.
Decision-making
How you weigh trade-offs and decide.
Technical design discussion
A project from your resume: the design, why you chose it, the alternatives, how it scaled and what you would do differently.
prep: Choose one project you know end to end and draw its architecture.
Write three key decisions, each with the alternative you rejected and why.
Know its numbers: volume, latency, cost, team size, timeline.
Have an honest answer to: what would you do differently?

rounds.s: Write correct SQL against a schema in 15 to 20 minutes a question, talking through it, then make it fast.
look: Correct first
Window functions, joins, deduplication, sessionization, top N per group, cohorts and funnels, all with NULLs and ties handled.
Speed
Two to four questions in a round; a clean first answer beats a clever late one.
Thinking out loud
State the grain of every subquery and check row counts as you go.
Optimising
Read a plan: partition pruning, join order, avoiding a shuffle, pre-aggregating.
prep: Do the Hard SQL problems under a timer, one a day.
Learn the eight patterns below until you can write each from memory.
Before typing, say the output grain: one row per what?
After it works, say one way to make it cheaper on a billion rows.

rounds.s: Model a product from a short prompt: grain, facts, dimensions, keys and history, then answer questions with it.
look: Grain
One row per what, stated first, for every table.
Facts and dimensions
Which events or snapshots are facts, which attributes describe them, and which facts are additive.
Keys and history
Surrogate keys, slowly changing dimension choices with a reason, late-arriving data.
Use
The model answers the business questions in the prompt with simple SQL.
prep: Ask what questions the model must answer before drawing anything.
Say the grain of each table out loud before its columns.
Pick an SCD type per attribute and say why.
Finish by writing one query the business asked for against your model.

rounds.s: Define how to measure a product, design the events to log, build the pipeline, then diagnose a metric that moved. Meta's data engineering loop runs this round.
look: Goal and metrics
A north-star metric tied to the product's goal, a few supporting metrics and a guardrail.
Logging
The events and fields to log, with ids and timestamps that make the metric computable.
Pipeline
Raw events to a fact table to daily aggregates, with late data and deduplication handled.
Diagnosis
A metric dropped: check the data first, then segment, then the product.
prep: Start from the user and the goal, not the dashboard.
Name one guardrail for every metric you push.
Write the event schema as a short table: event, fields, when it fires.
For a drop: is it real (logging, pipeline, definition), where is it (segment), why (product, outside).

recruiter.tip: Now, before, best win, why this role. 60 to 90 seconds. Use your pitch.

recruiter.q: What do you do in your current role, day to day?
recruiter.tip: Scope (team, systems, data volume), what you own, one recent result.

recruiter.q: Walk me through the project on your resume you are proudest of.
recruiter.tip: Problem, your part, the design in one sentence, the result with a number.

recruiter.q: What is your strongest technical area, and what are you still building?
recruiter.tip: Be specific; name what you are learning now and how.

recruiter.q: Which tools and languages have you used most in the last two years?
recruiter.tip: Group them: languages, processing, storage, cloud, orchestration. Say where you went deep.

recruiter.q: Why are you looking to move now?
recruiter.tip: Positive and forward-looking: what you want more of, never complaints.

recruiter.q: Why this company and this role?
recruiter.tip: One thing about the product, one about the scale or the team, one about what you bring.

recruiter.q: What kind of team and manager do you work best with?
recruiter.tip: Concrete habits: design reviews, ownership, clear goals.

recruiter.q: What is your notice period, and are you interviewing elsewhere?
recruiter.tip: Honest and short. Mention other processes if they affect the timeline.
Give a researched range for the level, or ask for theirs first; stay flexible on the mix.

recruiter.q: Do you have any questions for me?
recruiter.tip: Always yes: the interview loop, the team's biggest challenge, how success is measured in the first six months.

dsaSteps: Restate the problem. Ask about input size, duplicates, negatives, empty input, and what to return.
Work one small example by hand, and one edge case.
Say a brute force first, its complexity, then the better idea. Get a nod before coding.
State time and space for the approach you will code.
Write clean code with clear names, talking as you go.
Run your examples through the code line by line; fix bugs calmly.
Faster, less memory, streaming input, input that does not fit in memory, many machines.

cx.why: One pass; a set lookup and insert are O(1) on average. Space is O(n) for the set.
Every pair is compared: n(n-1)/2 comparisons. Space O(1).
Binary search halves the range each step.
Sorting dominates. A heap of size 10 would make it O(n log 10), which is O(n).

cx.code:
def first(rows):
    return rows[0] if rows else None
cx.why: Indexing a Python list is constant time.
n is the total number of words: each is touched once, dict updates are O(1) on average.
'in' on a list scans it, so n lookups of O(n) each. Turn known into a set to make it O(n).
A heap of size k is kept while scanning n items. With k fixed and small this is close to O(n).
Each call makes two more, recomputing the same values. Memoise it (or loop) for O(n).
One pass with O(1) work per item; append is amortised O(1).

cx.code:
def merge_sorted(a, b):
    return sorted(a + b)
cx.why: Correct but it ignores that a and b are already sorted. A two-pointer merge is O(n).
With n cells, each is enqueued and visited at most once (O(rows × cols)).

cc.spec: Keep readings that are zero or more, in order. None means a missing reading and is skipped.
cc.fixed:
def clean_readings(readings):
    return [r for r in readings if r is not None and r >= 0]

c: Return the readings that are zero or more, in order, skipping missing ones

cc.edge: A reading of 0 is valid but `> 0` drops it, and a None reading crashes the comparison in Python 3.

better.q: After the fix, which change makes it clearer without changing behaviour?
c: Loop over the values directly (or use a list comprehension) instead of indexes
better.why: Iterating over values removes the index bookkeeping, which is where off-by-one bugs hide.

cc.spec: Keep the most recently updated row for each id (highest updated_at), returned in id order.

what.q: What is this, in data engineering terms?
c: A deduplication that keeps the latest version of each row

cc.edge: The comparison is reversed, so it keeps the oldest row. Ties on updated_at keep the first one seen; say whether that is acceptable.

better.q: This runs on 500 million rows nightly. What would you do?
c: Do it in the engine: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1, or a MERGE
Add more RAM to the machine
Sort the rows in Python first
better.why: The warehouse or Spark does this in parallel; a Python dict of every id may not fit in memory.

cc.spec: Split items into batches of n. The last batch may be smaller.
cc.fixed:
def batches(items, n):
    return [items[i:i + n] for i in range(0, len(items), n)]

what.q: What does it return for 5 items and n = 2 today?
c: Two batches: the fifth item is silently dropped

cc.edge: The range stops before a partial batch, so the tail of the data is lost without any error: the worst kind of data bug.

better.q: The input is a 50 GB file streamed line by line. What changes?
c: Make it a generator that yields each batch, so it works on any iterable without holding it all
Read the file into a list first
better.why: A generator (or itertools.batched in Python 3.12) keeps memory constant.

cc.spec: Return a new list holding the event's type, added to the tags passed in (none by default).
cc.fixed:
def add_tag(event, tags=None):
    return list(tags or []) + [event["type"]]

what.q: What happens on the second call with no tags?
c: It returns only the second type
It returns both types: the default list is shared between calls

cc.edge: A default list is created once, when the function is defined, so every call shares it. The function also changes the caller's list.

better.q: How do you stop this class of bug coming back?
c: A linter rule (for example ruff B006) and a test that calls it twice
Comments asking people not to do it
better.why: Tools catch it on every change; a comment does not.

cc.spec: Return the mean of the latencies, or None when there are none.
cc.fixed:
def avg_latency(ms):
    return sum(ms) / len(ms) if ms else None

c: A minute with no requests: division by zero

cc.edge: An empty window is normal (a quiet minute), and it crashes the job.

better.q: The dashboard shows this average and users still complain about slowness. Why?
c: An average hides the slow tail; report p95 or p99 too
better.why: A few very slow requests barely move the mean but are what users feel.

cc.spec: Timestamps are minutes. A gap of more than 30 minutes starts a new session. Return how many sessions there are.
cc.edge: The boundary: the spec says more than 30, the code says 30 or more. Always test the exact boundary.

better.q: Events arrive late from phones that were offline. What changes in a streaming job?
c: Use event time with a watermark and allowed lateness, and merge sessions when a late event bridges a gap
Use the time the event arrived
better.why: Session windows in Flink or Spark merge when late data closes a gap.

cc.spec: Add each order's customer country; use "unknown" when the customer is missing. Keep every order.

what.q: In SQL terms this should be…
c: A left join from orders to customers

cc.edge: A late-arriving customer (the order came before the customer row) raises KeyError and stops the whole batch.

better.q: In a star schema, how do you handle the missing customer?
c: Point the fact at an 'unknown' member of the dimension and fix it up when the customer arrives
better.why: Facts are never lost and totals stay right; a later pass re-points the key.

cc.spec: Ignore None values; return how many values there are and their total.

c: A generator can be read only once; counting used it up

cc.edge: No error, just a wrong number: the generator is exhausted after the first pass.

better.q: Which fix keeps memory constant for a huge input?
c: One loop that counts and sums together
list() the generator, then use it twice
better.why: A list works but holds everything in memory; one pass does not.

cc.spec: Remove keys whose value is None or an empty string, and return the record.
cc.fixed:
def drop_empty(record):
    return {k: v for k, v in record.items() if v not in (None, "")}

what.q: What happens when a field is empty?
c: RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration

cc.edge: Deleting from a dict while looping over it raises. Note also: 0 and False must be kept, so do not test truthiness.

better.q: Should the function change the caller's dict?
c: Better to return a new dict, so callers are not surprised
Yes, always change inputs in place
better.why: Pure functions are easier to test and safe to retry.

cc.spec: Call fetch up to `tries` times. Return the first success; if every try fails, raise the last error.
tests:
calls = []
def f():
    calls.append(1)
    if len(calls) < 2:
        raise ValueError('down')
    return 'ok'
fetch_with_retry(f)

what.q: What does it do when the service is down for good?
c: Returns None silently: callers think it worked

cc.edge: attempt runs 0 to tries - 1, so attempt == tries is never true and failures are swallowed.

better.q: What else does a production retry need?
c: Exponential backoff with jitter, retry only errors that can pass, and an idempotent call
better.why: Without backoff, retries from many clients make an outage worse (a thundering herd).

cc.spec: Return the k most viewed pages, most viewed first.
cc.edge: sorted() is ascending by default. Also decide how ties are ordered so results are stable.

better.q: Views are a never-ending stream of billions. What would you use?
c: A count-min sketch with a small heap (approximate top k), or windowed counts in a stream processor
Keep a dict of every page forever
better.why: Exact counts of everything do not fit; approximate top k uses fixed memory.

cc.spec: Pages are numbered from 1. Return the rows on page page_no with `size` rows per page.

c: The second page: the first rows are never shown

cc.edge: Off by one: pages start at 1 but the offset assumes 0.

better.q: The API pages through a table that changes while users scroll. What is safer?
c: Keyset (cursor) pagination: WHERE id > last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT size
better.why: Offsets skip or repeat rows when rows are inserted, and get slower deep into the table.

aiq.q: You may use an AI assistant. What do you give it first?
c: The function, the spec, the input that fails and what you expected
Nothing: read the answer from it and paste it in
aiq.why: Specific context gets a specific answer; you stay in charge of the reasoning.

aiq.q: The assistant suggests rewriting the whole function. What do you do?
c: Ask for the smallest change that fixes the failing case, then decide
Accept it: it is probably right
aiq.why: Small changes are easier to review and less likely to break other behaviour.

aiq.q: The assistant's fix passes your one test. Are you done?
c: No: run the edge cases too (empty, boundary, missing data) and read the diff
Ask the assistant if it is right
aiq.why: Interviewers watch whether you verify, not whether you trust.

aiq.q: How do you talk about the AI's help to the interviewer?
c: Say what you asked, what it got right, what you changed and why
aiq.why: They assess how you use the tool: judgement, checking and ownership.

What you had to do, and why it was hard.
What you did, step by step. Say I, not we. Most of the story goes here.
What changed, with a number, and what you learned.

proj: Who had the problem, what it cost them, the numbers (volume, latency, money).
What you owned: design, build, team, decisions. Be exact.
The data or request flow from source to user, in a few lines. Draw it in the simulator.
What you chose, the alternative you rejected, and why.
What you chose, the alternative you rejected, and why.
What you chose, the alternative you rejected, and why.
Before and after numbers. What happens at ten times the load?
What broke, how you found out, what you changed.
Honest, specific, and what you learned.

What was the hardest technical problem, and how did you solve it?
What happens at ten times the data volume?
Where is the single point of failure?
How did you know it was working? What did you measure?

topics.t: 1 million events a second, exactly once
fr: Ingest app and device events at 1 million a second at peak
Enrich and aggregate them within seconds for a serving store
Land every event in the lake for replay and analytics
nfr: End to end in under 10 seconds
No event counted twice or lost (exactly-once results)
Survive a broker or zone loss
api: Producers write to Kafka with a schema checked by a registry
Consumers read with their own offsets
data: Topic keyed by user or device id; about 1 KB an event, so about 1 GB/s in
Serving store keyed by entity and window; lake tables partitioned by hour
decide: Partitions: a partition handles roughly 10 MB/s, so 1 GB/s needs 100 or more; plan for 2 to 3 times that for peaks and growth
Exactly once: idempotent producers, transactional or checkpointed writes (Flink two-phase commit) and idempotent upserts in the sink
Hot keys: salt or pre-aggregate the few huge keys; a DLQ for bad records

est.note: Each event is about 1 KB, kept in the lake, and read by two consumers.

fr: Stream every change from regional OLTP databases into a global lake and a search index
Keep a current-state copy within a minute
Rebuild any table from history
nfr: No lost or reordered changes per row
A region outage must not stop the others
api: Debezium reads each database log into a regional Kafka
Mirroring (MirrorMaker 2 or cluster linking) copies topics to the central region
data: Change events keyed by primary key, with source region, LSN and operation
Current-state tables built by MERGE on the key, keeping the highest LSN
decide: Log-based CDC over dual writes or polling (no deletes missed, no load on the app)
Order per key from the key-based partitioning and the LSN, not arrival time
Schema changes through a registry; snapshots for new tables; WAL retention sized for connector downtime

est.note: Each change is about 500 bytes, kept as history, and sent to three consumers (lake, search, other regions).

fr: Recompute three years of a core fact table after a logic fix
Keep daily jobs and dashboards running while it runs
Swap the new data in without readers seeing half of it
nfr: Restartable: a failure redoes only one partition
api: The same job code as the daily run, given a date range
An orchestrator runs it one partition (day) at a time, with a concurrency limit
data: About 2.5 PB a year of events: one partition per day, files of 256 MB to 1 GB
Writes to a new table version, swapped atomically (Iceberg or Delta snapshot) or partition by partition
decide: Idempotent per partition: overwrite a day, never append
Throttle so the daily SLA keeps priority; use spot capacity with retries
Validate counts and sums per partition against the old table before the swap

est.note: Each event is about 200 bytes; a backfill reads each byte once.
est.bwl: Data read a second for one pass of one year (average)

fr: Serve features for model scoring in under 10 ms
Give training the same features as of each past moment
Let teams define a feature once and reuse it
nfr: p99 under 10 ms at 100,000 reads a second
Fresh within minutes for streaming features
api: GET features(entity_id, feature_list) for online scoring
A point-in-time join for training sets
data: Online store: key-value by entity, latest value only
Offline store: lake tables of every value with event time
decide: One definition computes both stores (batch and streaming), so values match
Point-in-time correct joins in training (no future leakage)
Size the online store for a cold cache; TTLs for stale features

est.note: About 1 in 10 lookups is matched by a feature update of about 2 KB; a lookup returns about 2 KB.

fr: Move 2 PB and 4,000 jobs from a warehouse to Iceberg tables
Keep dashboards and SLAs working throughout
Cut cost by at least a third
nfr: Numbers match to the cent before cut-over
A rollback path for every step
api: Engines read the same Iceberg tables through one catalog
Jobs move one domain at a time
data: Tables partitioned by date, files compacted to 512 MB
A dual-run period writing both systems, with diff checks
decide: Strangler pattern: domain by domain, with dual runs and automatic diffs
Catalog and access control first, then data, then jobs, then dashboards
Measure cost per query before and after, and keep hot marts where they are cheaper

est.note: 1 in 20 queries writes about 50 MB; a query scans about 2 GB.
est.bwl: Data scanned a second on average

fr: Create a short link for a long URL
Redirect a short link to the long URL
Optional: custom alias, expiry, click counts
nfr: Links must never collide or disappear
api: POST /links {url} -> {code}
GET /{code} -> 302 Location: url
data: links(code PK, url, owner, created_at, expires_at)
clicks are an event stream, counted separately
decide: Code generation: base62 of a counter (no collisions, guessable) or a hash with a collision check
301 (cached by browsers, no counts) or 302 (every click counted)
Cache the hottest codes; size the store for a cold cache

est.note: 1 in 100 requests creates a link (about 500 bytes stored); a redirect sends about 500 bytes.

fr: One-to-one and group messages
Online status and read receipts
History synced across devices
nfr: Messages in order within a conversation
api: WebSocket: send {conv, text, client_msg_id}
GET /conv/{id}/messages?before=...
data: messages(conv_id, ts, msg_id, sender, text) partitioned by conv_id
presence in a cache with a short expiry
decide: WebSockets (push) over polling
Order per conversation: Kafka key = conversation id
Fan-out on write for small groups, on read for huge ones

est.note: Every message is stored (about 200 bytes) and delivered to two devices on average (400 bytes out).

fr: Drivers share their location
Riders see nearby drivers and request a ride
Match a rider to a driver and track the trip
api: POST /drivers/{id}/location {lat, lng} every 4 s
POST /rides {from, to} -> ride id
WebSocket for trip updates
data: geo index: cell -> drivers (in memory, expires fast)
trips(id, rider, driver, state, times) in a database
decide: Geo cells (geohash or H3) in a key-value store, not a SQL range query
Location updates are disposable; trips are durable: two different stores
Partition by city or region

est.note: Users here are drivers, sending a location every 4 seconds for an hour a day; each update is about 100 bytes, kept and served once.

fr: Upload a video
Watch it on any device at the right quality
Search and recommendations (mention, do not design)
api: POST /uploads -> signed URL to object storage
GET /videos/{id}/manifest -> chunk list per quality
data: videos(id, owner, title, status)
chunks in object storage: video/quality/segment
decide: Adaptive bitrate: many qualities, small chunks
CDN for delivery; object storage as origin with a shield cache
Queue and workers for transcoding

est.note: 1 in 100 views is matched by an upload of about 500 MB across all qualities; a view streams about 100 MB.

aiTopics.t: RAG over 10 million documents at 1,000 questions a second
fr: Answer questions from 10 million internal documents, with citations
Only retrieve what the asking user may read
Reflect document changes within minutes
nfr: First token within about 1.5 seconds (p95), answer streamed
Grounded: say so when the documents do not answer it
api: POST /ask (question, user) through the gateway; streamed answer with numbered citations
Document change events re-embed only the changed chunks
data: About 40 million chunks of 500 tokens, vectors of 1,024 dimensions (160 GB as float32), sharded and replicated, with the permission list stored on each chunk
A semantic cache keyed by question embedding; traces with tokens, latency and retrieved chunk ids
decide: Hybrid retrieval (vector plus keyword, rank fusion), then a cross-encoder rerank of the top 50
The model is the latency and cost budget: semantic cache, prompt caching and routing easy questions to a small model
Groundedness on a golden set before every prompt, model or index change

aiTopics.t: A support agent with tools and handoff to a person
fr: Answer customers in chat and look up their orders
Refund and cancel within policy
Hand the conversation to a person with its full history
nfr: Never act twice; never refund over the limit without approval
Every turn traced: model calls, tool calls, tokens
api: Read tools inline (order status); write tools and handoff as queued jobs with idempotency keys
An approval step for refunds over the limit
data: Conversation history and the agent's notes per conversation
A golden set of conversations with the expected outcome and tool calls
decide: One agent with a short tool list; several agents only if the work splits into independent parts
Guardrails in the tools (limits, ownership checks), not only in the prompt; tool results and customer text are data, never instructions
Evals on resolution and wrong-action rate as a gate for every change

fr: One door to every model for every team
Quotas and monthly budgets per team, spend reported per team
Survive a provider outage
nfr: Adds only milliseconds to each call
No provider key outside the gateway

sqlPat: Latest row per key
Deduplicate CDC or events to current state.

SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT t.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, seq DESC) AS rn
  FROM t) x
WHERE rn = 1
Top N per group
Best sellers per category, top drivers per city.

SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT city, driver_id, trips, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY trips DESC) AS r
  FROM driver_trips) x
WHERE r <= 3
Running total and moving average
Cumulative revenue, 7-day averages.

SELECT day, rev,
  SUM(rev) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS cum_rev,
  AVG(rev) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS avg_7d
FROM daily_rev
Gaps and islands
Streaks of consecutive active days.

SELECT user_id, MIN(d) AS start_d, MAX(d) AS end_d FROM (
  SELECT user_id, d, d - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY d) * INTERVAL '1 day' AS grp
  FROM active_days) x
GROUP BY user_id, grp
Sessionization
A new session after 30 minutes idle.

SELECT *, SUM(new_s) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) AS session_no FROM (
  SELECT *, CASE WHEN ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) <= INTERVAL '30 minutes' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS new_s
  FROM events) x
Retention by cohort
Of users who joined in a week, how many came back in week N.

SELECT c.cohort_wk, DATE_DIFF('week', c.cohort_wk, DATE_TRUNC('week', a.d)) AS wk_n, COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS users
FROM cohorts c JOIN active_days a USING (user_id)
GROUP BY 1, 2
Funnel
View, then add to cart, then purchase, in order.

SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE v IS NOT NULL) AS viewed,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE c > v) AS carted,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p > c) AS bought
FROM (SELECT user_id, MIN(ts) FILTER (WHERE e='view') v, MIN(ts) FILTER (WHERE e='cart') c, MIN(ts) FILTER (WHERE e='buy') p
      FROM events GROUP BY user_id) x
As-of join to an SCD2 dimension
The customer's segment at the time of each order.

SELECT o.order_id, d.segment
FROM orders o JOIN dim_customer d
  ON o.customer_id = d.customer_id
 AND o.order_ts >= d.valid_from AND o.order_ts < COALESCE(d.valid_to, TIMESTAMP '9999-12-31')

model.q: Model trips for a ride-hailing company. The business wants completed trips and gross bookings by city and day, driver earnings per week, and cancellation rates by rider segment.

a.ask: Is a cancelled request a trip? Which currency? How late can a trip change (tips, refunds days later)? Do we need history of a driver's vehicle or rating?
a.grain: fact_trip: one row per trip request (trip_id), whatever its outcome, with status. fact_trip_payment: one row per payment event (charge, tip, refund). fact_driver_week: a periodic snapshot, one row per driver per week.
a.facts: fact_trip: fare, distance_km, duration_min, surge (additive except surge, an average). fact_trip_payment: amount in local currency and USD (additive). Bookings come from payments, so late tips and refunds land as new rows rather than updates.
a.dims: dim_date (role-playing: request, pickup, payment), dim_city, dim_rider (Type 2 on segment and home city, Type 1 on email), dim_driver (Type 2 on vehicle and tier), dim_product (UberX, Pool). Flags such as airport or scheduled as booleans or a junk dimension.
a.keys: Surrogate keys on every dimension; the fact carries the surrogate key valid at request time. trip_id is the degenerate dimension. An unknown member (-1) for late-arriving drivers or riders, re-pointed when they arrive.
a.query: Gross bookings by city and day: SUM(amount_usd) from fact_trip_payment joined to dim_city and dim_date on payment_date_key, grouped by city and day.

rubric: Stated the grain of every table first
Separated trips from payments (late money is new rows)
Chose an SCD type per attribute with a reason
Used surrogate keys and an unknown member
Answered a business question with SQL

model.q: Model ads delivery: advertisers want impressions, clicks, spend and conversions per campaign per hour, and attribution of conversions to the last click within 7 days.

a.ask: Billions of impressions a day: do we keep every impression or aggregate? Attribution window and model? Do conversions come from the advertiser later? Time zone of reporting?
a.grain: fact_impression: one row per impression (often kept 30 to 90 days, then aggregated). fact_click: one row per click, with impression_id. fact_conversion: one row per conversion event, with the attributed click_id. agg_campaign_hour: one row per ad per hour.
a.facts: Impressions and clicks are counts (additive); spend is additive; CTR and CPC are ratios computed from sums, never stored as averages to add up.
a.dims: dim_advertiser, dim_campaign, dim_ad_set, dim_ad (Type 2 on budget and targeting, so reports show settings at the time), dim_placement, dim_device, dim_date and dim_hour.
a.keys: impression_id and click_id as degenerate keys linking the facts. Attribution runs as a job that joins conversions to the last click within 7 days and writes the click_id onto the conversion; late conversions re-run the affected days.
a.query: CTR per campaign per day: SUM(clicks) / NULLIF(SUM(impressions), 0) from agg_campaign_hour joined to dim_campaign, grouped by campaign and day.

rubric: Kept event grain and an hourly aggregate, and said why
Computed ratios from sums, not stored averages
Kept campaign settings as of the time (Type 2)

model.q: Model a sales pipeline. Leaders want pipeline value by stage at the end of each week, how long deals sit in each stage, and win rate by sales rep and region over time.

a.ask: Can a deal move backwards? Does the region of a rep change? Do we need pipeline as it was on any past date? Multiple currencies?
a.grain: fact_opportunity_snapshot: one row per opportunity per day (or week), a periodic snapshot. fact_stage_change: one row per stage transition. An accumulating snapshot with one row per opportunity and a date per milestone also works for stage durations.
a.facts: Amount is semi-additive: sum it across opportunities, never across days (take the last day of the week). Days in stage comes from stage changes.
a.dims: dim_rep (Type 2 on region and team, so win rate counts the region at the time), dim_account (Type 2 on segment), dim_stage, dim_product, dim_date.
a.keys: Surrogate keys; opportunity_id as a degenerate dimension. Rep changes produce a new dim_rep row, and the snapshot row points at the version valid that day.
a.query: Pipeline by stage at week end: SUM(amount) from the snapshot WHERE snapshot_date is the last day of each week, grouped by week and stage.

rubric: Chose a periodic or accumulating snapshot and said why
Answered 'as it was on a date'

model.q: Model an online store: revenue by product and day, return rates by category, and how much each customer spends in their first 90 days.

a.ask: Partial shipments and returns? Discounts at order or line level? Do product categories change? Is a customer anonymous before sign-up?
a.grain: fact_order_line: one row per order line item. fact_return_line: one row per returned item. A customer daily snapshot is optional; first-90-day spend can be computed from order lines.
a.facts: Quantity, gross amount, discount and net amount per line (additive). Order-level shipping is allocated to lines, or kept in a separate order-grain fact.
a.dims: dim_product (Type 2 on category and price band), dim_customer (Type 2 on segment; first_order_date as an attribute), dim_date, dim_promotion, dim_channel.
a.keys: Surrogate keys; order_id and line number as degenerate dimensions; returns carry the original order line's id.
a.query: Return rate by category: returned units divided by sold units from the two facts joined to dim_product, grouped by category.

rubric: Handled returns as their own fact

model.q: Model a music streaming service: plays per artist per day for royalty payments, subscriber counts by plan at month end, and churn.

a.ask: What counts as a play (30 seconds?). Are royalties paid on plays per country? Can a user change plan mid-month? Offline plays arrive days later?
a.grain: fact_play: one row per qualifying play. fact_subscription_day or month: a periodic snapshot, one row per subscriber per day or month. fact_subscription_event: one row per start, change, cancel.
a.facts: Play count and seconds (additive). Subscribers are counted from the snapshot (semi-additive across time). Churn = cancels in month / subscribers at month start.
a.dims: dim_track, dim_artist (a bridge table for tracks with several artists, with weights for royalty splits), dim_user (Type 2 on country and plan), dim_plan, dim_device, dim_date.
a.keys: Surrogate keys; offline plays are accepted late and the royalty month recomputed for affected days; play_id deduplicates replays from devices.
a.query: Plays per artist per day: SUM(plays × weight) from fact_play joined through the artist bridge, grouped by artist and day.

rubric: Used a bridge for many artists
Snapshot for subscribers, events for churn
Royalty query uses the split weights

metrics.q: A photo app launched Stories. How do you know if it is working? Design the metrics, the logging and the pipeline.

a.goal: Stories should get people sharing more often and coming back. Success is more people sharing and viewing without hurting feed engagement.
a.metrics: North star: daily users who post or view a story. Supporting: stories posted per poster, views per story, share of viewers who reply. Guardrails: feed time per user, app crashes, reports per story.
a.events: story_post(user_id, story_id, ts, media_type, device), story_view(viewer_id, story_id, author_id, ts, seconds_viewed), story_reply(user_id, story_id, ts), with an app session_id on every event and a client event_id to deduplicate.
a.pipeline: Client events to a Kafka topic, landed hourly in the lake; dedupe by event_id; fact_story_view at event grain; daily aggregates per user and per country; a dashboard and an experiment table joined to assignment.
a.sql: Daily story users: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) over story_post and story_view events per day.
a.diag: If views drop 10%: check logging (new app version, missing events, pipeline lag), then segment by country, platform, version and new versus old users, then product changes and seasonality.

rubric: North star, supporting and a guardrail
Events with ids, timestamps and dedup keys
Pipeline handles late and duplicate events

metrics.q: Customers complain that the estimated delivery time is wrong. Define how to measure it, log it and report it.

a.goal: Estimates should be close to what happens, and rarely late, because lateness hurts more than earliness.
a.metrics: Share of orders delivered within ±5 minutes of the estimate shown at checkout; p50 and p90 absolute error; share late by more than 10 minutes. Guardrails: conversion at checkout (padding estimates lowers it), courier utilisation.
a.events: eta_shown(order_id, ts, eta_min, model_version, stage), order_placed, picked_up, delivered(order_id, ts), all with city and restaurant ids.
a.pipeline: Join the estimate shown at checkout to the actual delivery per order (late delivered events allowed up to a day), compute error per order in fact_order_eta, aggregate daily by city and model version.
a.sql: Within five minutes: AVG(CASE WHEN ABS(actual_min - eta_min) <= 5 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) per city and day.
a.diag: If accuracy drops: a new model version, a city with weather or events, restaurants with slow prep, missing delivered events making orders look late.

rubric: Joined estimate to actual per order

metrics.q: A CRM shipped an AI assistant inside the deal page. Leadership asks: is it being adopted, and is it helping sales teams?

a.goal: Reps should use the assistant regularly and close deals faster or more often; admins must trust it.
a.metrics: Adoption: weekly active reps using it / reps with access, by account. Value: deal cycle time and win rate for users versus matched non-users, or in an experiment by account. Guardrails: suggestions dismissed, support tickets, data-access errors.
a.events: assistant_open(user_id, org_id, opp_id, ts), suggestion_shown(suggestion_id, type), suggestion_accepted or dismissed, with org_id on every event for per-customer reporting and tenant isolation.
a.pipeline: Events per tenant into the lake, deduplicated; join to opportunity stage history; weekly adoption per org; an experiment or a matched comparison for value.
a.sql: Weekly adoption: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) of assistant users / COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) with access, per org per week.
a.diag: If adoption stalls: which orgs (enabled but unused?), which roles, did a release break the entry point, are suggestions dismissed (quality)?

rubric: Chose a fair comparison or experiment

metrics.q: The team wants to send more push notifications. How would you measure whether that is good for the product?

a.goal: Notifications should bring people back to something they value, without making them turn notifications off.
a.metrics: Primary: sessions started from a notification that last more than 30 seconds, per user per week. Guardrails: notification opt-out rate, uninstalls, long-term retention (four weeks).
a.events: notif_sent(notif_id, user_id, type, ts), notif_opened(notif_id, ts), session_start(user_id, ts, source), notif_settings_changed(user_id, type, on/off).
a.pipeline: Join sends to opens and sessions by notif_id within a window; daily per type; an A/B test on volume with a holdout group kept for months.
a.sql: Open rate per type: COUNT(opened) / COUNT(sent) grouped by type and day.
a.diag: If opt-outs rise: which notification type, which country, new users versus old, a change in frequency caps.

rubric: Linked sends to opens by id
